description.narrative:
Internationella Brottmålsdomstolen (ICC) i Haag har mandat att utreda och lagföra de allvarligaste internationella brotten: folkmord, brott mot mänskligheten, krigsförbrytelser och aggressionsbrott (kallade brott enligt Romstadgan).
ICC Trust Fund for Victims (TFV) inrättades 2004 av statsparterna till ICC för att tillsammans med ICC bilda Romstadgans pelare för reparativ rättvisa – vilken arbetar för att reparativ rättvisa och rätten till skadestånd för brott enligt Romstadgan ska bli verklighet för offren och deras familjer, och därigenom mildra effekterna av sådana skador och arbeta för fred och stabilitet.
TFV:s mandat omfattar både domstolsbeslutad ersättning, kopplad till en fällande dom i ett mål inför ICC, och andra bredare reparativa åtgärder i förhållande till ICC:s allmänna jurisdiktion i ett situationsland. TFV:s program är utformat kring det huvudsakliga strategiska målet att det "leder till att offren, deras familjer och samhällen övervinner skador som lidits till följd av brott enligt Romstadgan". Detta återspeglar ett tillvägagångssätt som sätter offren i centrum och som utgår från deras samhällsdeltagande, validering samt ett jämställdhetsperspektiv.
Portföljen omfattar för närvarande fyra domstolsbeslutade skadeståndsprogram: Katanga (DRK), Lubanga (DRK), Ntaganda (DRK) och Al Mahdi (Mali) samt sju ICC-länder (Uganda, Kenya, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Centralafrikanska republiken, Elfenbenskusten, Mali och Georgien).

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has the mandate to investigate and prosecute the most serious crimes of concern to the international community: the crimes of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression (referred to as Rome Statute crimes).
The ICC Trust Fund for Victims (TFV) was created by the Assembly of States Parties in 2004 in order to form, jointly with the ICC, the pillar of reparative justice of the Rome Statute - working to make reparative justice and the right to reparations for Rome Statute crimes a reality for victims and their families, thereby mitigating the impact of such harm and working towards peace and stability.
The TFV's mandate includes both court-ordered reparations, linked to a conviction in a case before the ICC, and other broader reparative measures in relation to ICC's general jurisdiction in a situation country. The TFV programme is designed around the main strategic objective of "programmes lead to victims, their families and communities overcoming harm suffered as result of Rome Statute crimes". This reflects a victim-centered approach enabled by community participation, validation and a gender perspective.
The TFV portfolio is currently covering four court-ordered reparation programmes: Katanga (DRC), Lubanga (DRC), Ntaganda (DRC) and Al Mahdi (Mali), as well as seven ICC situation countries (Uganda, Kenya, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Central African Republic, Cote d’Ivoire, Mali, and Georgia).

The TFV Strategic Plan 2023-2025, is centered around the following main strategic goal: TFV programmes lead to victims, their families and communities overcoming harm suffered as result of Rome Statute crimes
This main strategic goal reflects the two-fold TFV mandate as well as a victim-centred and harm-based approach, which is enabled by community participation and validation, as well as by gender sensitive programming.
The TFV strategic plan then outlines four additional goals which together cover programme development and communication, outreach to victims, knowledge management, partnership development, capacity building and advocacy, resource development, financial and fund management, governance, internal organisation, and human resource development. They also address the importance of strategies related to coordinated action with the ICC and the relationship between the TFV and the ICC:
- TFV programmes are perceived as part of the ICC justice system
- The TFVs expertise in designing and implementing transformative reparations is well-known at the international and national levels
- The TFV has adequate funds to operate its mandated activities.
- The TFVs agile organisation allows for low cost and sustainable TFV programmes

2024 is the second year under the current agreement period 2023-2025. The annual narrative report for 2024 accounts for activities and achieved results related to the four goals in the TFV strategic plan.
Below are a few examples of results achieved in 2024:
- In Ukraine, the TFV continued its engagement with the Ukraine authorities and with the Register of Damage for Ukraine, with a view to potential collaboration. The TFV also started to share experiences in different fora and build synergies as part of efforts to address the situation of victims in Ukraine. In November 2024, the TFV participated in a USAID conference on "Justice in the Domestic Adjudication of War Crimes Cases in Ukraine" and on compensation for damage, with a view to developing international and domestic relief mechanisms and measures in Ukraine. Moreover, the TFV exchanged with national reparation initiatives/providers in the country.
- In 2024, 2 896 victims directly benefitted from the TFV programme in the DRC through the provision of psychological care, medical treatment, and income-generating activities. In addition, during the reporting period, the TFVs assistance programme have supported peace education and reconciliation initiatives in 85 schools in North and South Kivu, reaching 53 262 students, fostering a culture of nonviolence, reconciliation, and respect for human rights in communities affected by Rome Statute crimes.
- Related to the evaluation of the Katanga programme (DRC), 79 % of victims who received reparations said that reparations brought justice. The level of satisfaction was slightly higher among men (70%) than women (67%). Similarly, victims who suffered material harm expressed higher satisfaction (79%) compared those who did not (50%). Furthermore, the results of the evaluation in the Katanga case also show that the reparations programme made an impact on trust in local and international institutions. This is because victims' sense of the delivery of reparations brought justice and that institutions recognised the harm they suffered and took actions to address their harm. Beneficiaries of reparations expressed greater trust in core institutions such as judiciary, government, and international actors compared to non-beneficiaries. These institutions are generally not highly trusted, but reparations appear to have contributed to improving the perceptions.
In Uganda, over 12,444 victims (8 228 female and 4 216 male) directly benefitted from either one or more services in ranging from medical treatment, corrective surgeries, psychotropic drugs, physiotherapy, counselling services (individual and family), group counselling, and socio-economic initiatives. Also, an external evaluation of the assistance programme in Uganda was concluded in 2024. Beneficiaries shared their stories of change, highlighting the impact of the TFVs mental health rehabilitation services. Their testimonies revealed that psychological rehabilitation was a significant factor in their healing and recovery process, offering a sense of dignity and a step toward redress for the harm they had suffered. Community leaders and other stakeholders who participated in evaluation such us administrators, government officials, medical professionals, and civil society organisations also voiced the tangible transformations they have observed among the beneficiaries and testified improvements in independence, reduced criminal behaviour, and increased economic activities.
- Through a range of individual and collective psychotherapy services in the Central African Republic (CAR), from 2020 to 2024, around 8 000 survivors of sexual and gender-based crimes (approximately 15 % male) with serious post-traumatic disorders, have shown improvement in their mental health and psychosocial well-being. In this same period, around 5 000 survivors living with severe health issues because of rape and sexual violence received medical care such as gynaecological reparative surgery through partnerships with 25 medical health centres and 977 individuals living with HIV/AIDS positive and undergoing antiretroviral treatment, have improved their physical condition after receiving dietary supplements and medication.
In relation to mobilisation of funds, which is key factor to be able to sustain as well as to respond to the current needs, efforts of the TFV and partners, including team Sweden, the European Parliament Resolution of 2 April 2025 on human rights and democracy in the world and the European Unions Policy on the matter (P10_TA(2025)0059), makes for the first time a specific reference to financial support to the Trust Fund for Victims when calling EU member states to continue providing support to the Court.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
